title: The World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA): Hardware-Algorithm Co-Design for Embedded AI in Robotics
summary: Embedded AI is moving from perception to prediction. Robots now use world models$\unicode{x2014}$learned simulators that predict the outcome of candidate actions in a compressed latent space before any is executed. Every predicted step must be computed on board within a tight power and thermal budget, yet the energy these steps fundamentally require, and how far real hardware sits from it, have not been characterized. We derive lower bounds on the arithmetic operations and the CMOS dynamic energy of a latent state transition from information theory and Boolean circuit complexity. Profiling a DreamerV3-style Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) shows that every rollout operation is memory-bandwidth bound and that a GPU consumes at least $5.9\times10^{10}$ times the CMOS energy floor. Transient 3D thermal simulations show that this inefficiency is also a thermal one, since sustained back-to-back planning heats a millimeter-scale silicon tile to 556 K even behind an ideal copper heat spreader. Guided by this chain from bound to bottleneck, we propose the World Model Planning Accelerator (WMPA), a chip architecture for embedded world model planning that combines near-memory computation, real-time entropy estimation, variable-precision rollout units, and copy-on-write latent scratchpads. With a design target of 40x lower power, the same tile stays near ambient at 306 K in simulation, pointing toward practical planning on thermally constrained robots.

title: PENSA: A Spatial Accelerator for BitNet b1.58 Inference on an HBM-equipped AMD Alveo FPGA
summary: Ternary large language models (tLLMs) replace general multiplication in dominant linear layers with sign-controlled accumulation, shifting hardware bottlenecks toward packed-weight delivery, reduction, and operator occupancy. PENSA is an end-to-end FPGA accelerator for the BitNet b1.58 2B4T model on an AMD Alveo U50. Two row-partitioned ternary matrix engines consume packed TQ1_0 weights from eight independent high-bandwidth memory (HBM) pseudo-channels, each processing 1,280 ternary weights per cycle through sign selection and integer reduction. The sequencer, attention, and vocabulary-projection units remain resident on the FPGA, while two-stream interleaved scheduling overlaps sequences across the persistent pipeline to form the Penta-Unit. At 104.1~MHz, PENSA achieves 58.09 tok/s at context 128 and 24.60 tok/s at context 2048, corresponding to 2.14-3.14$\times$ the throughput of a same-model Xeon E-2356G baseline. The resulting system demonstrates end-to-end FPGA execution of 2B-scale BitNet topology without modifying its model structure.

title: RTLREX: LLM-Guided Framework for Exact High-Level RTL Recovery
summary: Hardware designs may be available only as gate-level netlists or input-output descriptions when the original register-transfer-level (RTL) design and documentation are not accessible. Low-level representations obscure word-level computation and its finite-width behavior. Recovering high-level RTL from such representations therefore helps engineers understand a circuit's functionality and enables RTL rewriting and resynthesis. A plausible function model is also insufficient unless the generated RTL is equivalent to the original circuit for all input combinations. In this paper, we present RTLREX, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that coordinates domain-specific tools for function recovery, RTL generation, independent verification, and cost-guided rewriting. Independent verification establishes equivalence between the recovered RTL and the original circuit. The LLM uses tool feedback to select further analyses, revise candidate RTL, and propose syntax-cost reductions. Experiments on 30 benchmarks from Problem A of the ICCAD 2022 CAD Contest show that RTLREX recovers equivalent high-level RTL for all benchmarks, surpassing the state-of-the-art method WolFEx in recovery coverage. On benchmarks recovered by both methods, RTLREX reduces mean syntax cost by 20.5% relative to WolFEx. On complete truth-table benchmarks from the IWLS 2026 Contest, our framework reduces mean syntax cost by 95.7% relative to an LLM agent baseline on the benchmarks validated by both methods.

title: AutoC2V: Synthesis-Guided LLM Training for QoR-Optimized C++-to-Verilog Generation
summary: High-level synthesis (HLS) can translate C/C++ kernels into register-transfer level (RTL) designs, yet generating high-quality hardware still relies heavily on manual pragma tuning and repeated synthesis evaluation. We propose AutoC2V, a C++-to-Verilog generation framework driven by real synthesis feedback that enables large language models (LLMs) to directly generate RTL with improved quality of results (QoR) from synthesizable C++ kernels. We construct training data from real synthesis results, including synthesizable C++ source code, the corresponding Verilog RTL, QoR metrics, and optimization objectives. Using this dataset, we align the model toward synthesis-aware RTL generation through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To reduce the high cost of repeatedly invoking real synthesis during GRPO, we design the QoR Prediction Reward Model (QoR RM), which predicts latency and resource metrics by encoding RTL into long-context semantic representations, thereby providing low-cost and continuous QoR reward signals for policy optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that AutoC2V not only substantially improves RTL functional pass rates, but also achieves superior latency and resource optimization compared to the unfine-tuned base model, representative HLS optimization approaches (HLSPilot, LLM-DSE, and AutoDSE), and advanced general-purpose commercial models (Claude Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek v4 Pro, and GLM-5.2). These results indicate that combining real synthesis data with efficient QoR reward modeling can further improve the ability of LLMs to generate high-quality RTL.

title: Bit-level Perceptron Prediction for Indirect Branches
comment: Author manuscript of Proceedings of the 46th International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA '19), pp. 27-38 (2019). 12 manuscript pages plus publication-notice page
summary: Modern software uses indirect branches for various purposes including, but not limited to, virtual method dispatch and implementation of switch statements. Because an indirect branch's target address cannot be determined prior to execution, high-performance processors depend on highly-accurate indirect branch prediction techniques to mitigate control hazards. This paper proposes a new indirect branch prediction scheme that predicts target addresses at the bit level. Using a series of perceptron-based predictors, our predictor predicts individual branch target address bits based on correlations within branch history. Our evaluations show this new branch target predictor is competitive with state-of-the-art branch target predictors at an equivalent hardware budget. For instance, over a set of workloads including SPEC and mobile applications, our predictor achieves a misprediction rate of 0.183 mispredictions per 1000 instructions, compared with 0.193 for the state-of-the-art ITTAGE predictor and 0.29 for a VPC-based indirect predictor.

title: Augur: An Online Learning-based Hardware Data Prefetcher using Reservoir Computing
summary: Machine-learning-based hardware prefetchers can learn complex access patterns, but practical deployment demands online adaptation, low-latency inference, and modest hardware cost. We present Augur, a hardware delta prefetcher based on next-generation reservoir computing (NGRC) that meets all three requirements. Augur formulates delta prediction as a history-based regression problem. It constructs a fixed-size reservoir from hashed delta features over a short context window and predicts the next delta using a single dot product. The model is updated online via one-step SGD and requires no offline pre-training, no workload-specific tuning, and no floating-point arithmetic. A key technical insight makes this practical: replacing the integer multiplications traditionally used to generate nonlinear reservoir features with bitwise AND operations removes all feature-generation multipliers while preserving the joint context encoded in hash-derived features. Because Augur regresses a continuous delta rather than classifying into a fixed action set, it can predict any delta in [-64, 63]. Augur pairs the reservoir with a simple Markov-based delta predictor for simple delta patterns and employs multi-layered filtering and adaptive lookahead to suppress wasteful prefetches. Evaluated on 169 traces spanning GAP, Ligra, PARSEC, SPEC CPU 2006, SPEC CPU 2017, and AI workloads, Augur outperforms the state-of-the-art ML-based delta prefetcher by 2.9%, 4.5%, and 5.3% in geomean speedup on 1-, 4-, and 8-core systems, respectively, while achieving ~2x higher prefetch accuracy and 37.8% fewer overpredictions. Augur is practical to implement at 35 KB storage, 0.32 sq. mm area, and 32.7 mW in 12 nm.

title: Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies
comment: Accepted to IEEE International 3D Systems Integration Conference (3DIC)
summary: Recent generations of high bandwidth memory (HBM), such as HBM4, allow the base die of the memory stack to be manufactured using a logic process that can accommodate more complex controller functions next to the DRAM. We present the first systematic quantitative study of function-level controller placement between the host and the HBM4 base die on a silicon interposer. We divide the controller into its main functions and evaluate four placements, from a complete host controller to a complete base die controller, with intermediate placements that move maintenance or scheduling to the base die. We extend Ramulator 2 with HBM4 timing and maintenance, model a die-to-die (D2D) link with timing checks at the DRAM interface, and compose area, energy, and temperature from synthesized controller blocks, modeled storage, and interface data. A provisioned D2D link preserves per-stack bandwidth and adds about twice its one-way delay to unloaded latency. Maintenance moves to the base die with no bandwidth cost and frees host command slots, and the freed share grows with stack height. Replacing the wide interface with a D2D link saves 61% of host shoreline and 16.85 mm2 of host area per stack. The D2D link dominates the added base die area and power, and the base die runs cooler under streaming with link energy below 0.4 pJ/bit. Shared control delivers up to 1.72x the throughput of static partitioning between two requestors.

title: When Is High-Bandwidth Flash Cost-Effective for LLM Inference?
summary: Can high-bandwidth flash (HBF) make LLM inference cheaper than adding GPUs? By storing weights closer to the GPU than SSD, HBF may reduce the number of GPUs needed for model capacity. However, this integration is only justified if it meets service targets and its cost is recovered. We simulate this integration using public component data across nine dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, five workloads, two GPU platforms, and 1--100 GPUs. At fixed demand, HBF reduces the minimum GPU count to meet a service target in 98 of 468 comparisons; majority of them are paused and short sessions, 63 remain cost-effective at half a GPU price per HBF stack. For single short-chat users, HBF enables large MoEs, e.g. DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, to meet a relaxed service target on one RTX~4090 GPU, where conventional serving fails. At fixed GPU count, HBF improves throughput in 48\% of matched comparisons below 16 GPUs and 13\% at larger counts. Even at 100 RTX~4090-scale GPUs, cascaded HBF raises offline throughput by 16.4--26.5$\times$ for three large MoEs. We found savings and throughput gains arise in different scenarios.

title: PRISM: Preference-based Reward and Uncertainty-Integrated Synthesis Minimization for RTL PPA Optimization
summary: This paper introduces a budget-aware, multi-objective framework (called PRISM) for RTL optimization that improves power, performance, and area (PPA) while sharply limiting expensive commercial synthesis tool calls. Starting from a synthesizable baseline and functional testbench, the method iterates through LLM-driven rewrite generation, fast compile/simulation equivalence filtering, low-cost proxy feature extraction, and selective commercial synthesis tool (Synopsys Design Compiler (DC)) evaluation. To prioritize which candidates deserve high-quality synthesis, we train a preference-based reward model using pairwise ranking supervision derived from commercial synthesis tool outcomes, and combine ensemble uncertainty with a diversity-aware acquisition rule to avoid early bias and redundant evaluations. A key advantage is that PRISM maintains a best-tradeoff set G of non-dominated designs throughout the run: G preserves the best solutions found so far, is fed back into generation and refinement, and enables consistent, cumulative improvements rather than repeatedly restarting from the baseline. Across RTLLM v2.0 modules, the approach consistently yields post-synthesis gains under fixed commercial synthesis tool call budgets, and ablations confirm that reward-guided selection and candidate dropping are central to sample-efficient progress. PRISM efficacy is evaluated across multiple technology nodes (7 nm, 15 nm, and 45 nm) using identical pipelines without retraining.

title: Efficient VLA Inference via Retrieval-Based Speculation and Hardware Acceleration
summary:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to understand and execute complex instructions, but their autoregressive (AR) action generation introduces significant latency on resource-constrained robotic platforms. Speculative decoding can accelerate AR-based inference by parallelizing action generation and verification; however, existing approaches rely on costly draft models, which are inefficient on edge platforms.
  In this paper, we propose Zora, a hardware-software co-design framework for accelerating AR-based VLA inference. Specifically, Zora introduces a lightweight retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based draft model that exploits robotic dynamics without additional neural draft models. We further reduce batch verification overhead through a kinematics-guided action-acceptance strategy and a KV-cache-sharing attention mechanism. To address the retrieval overhead introduced by RAG-based drafting, we co-design dedicated hardware support, Zora core, to address the memory irregularity in RAG-based drafting. We evaluate Zora on four VLA models with the LIBERO benchmark. Zora retains comparable accuracy while achieving up to 3.4$\times$ speedup with software-only optimization and up to 7.6$\times$ speedup with hardware support over GPUs.

title: A Per-Step Load-Balancing Engine for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
comment: An anonymous version of this manuscript was submitted to HPCA 2027 on August 1, 2026. The original submission PDF and its SHA-256 checksum are archived at https://github.com/SuanNaiShuiGuoLao/relief-paper-archive
summary: In expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts serving, a layer finishes only when the most loaded GPU of its group does. Token routing shifts at every decode step and concentrates on a few experts, so most of the group's reserved GPU time waits on stragglers. Recovering that time means re-deciding, at every layer of every decode step, how each replicated expert's tokens divide between its copies. The exact linear-program solvers that make this decision optimally take longer than many of the layers they serve, and their working set outgrows GPU shared memory at deployment scale. We introduce Relief, a bidirectional pairwise relaxation that makes the linear program unnecessary, coming within a fraction of a point of the per-step optimum in a few passes of integer halving over the token counts. We build and measure three deployments, CUDA kernels on the serving GPU, the same verified engine on an FPGA over PCIe, and a fixed-function block beside the accelerator. On decode routing from three open MoE families, Relief holds the balance near the per-step optimum at every group size and layer time measured. Scored as effective utilization relative to that optimum, the kernel alone matches or exceeds every deployable scheme at every group size, from the hundred-microsecond layer on. The on-die engine widens that lead at every point, recovering up to 37.3 percentage points over the deployed static placement, while adding 0.02% of a current accelerator's transistors.

title: CU-3D: A Scalable Legality-Aware RTL-to-GDS Flow for 3D-IC Physical Design
summary: Face-to-face (F2F) hybrid bonds shorten interdie connections, but data, clock, and power-grid (PG) connections must be realized together. CU-3D is a RTL-to-GDS physical design flow based on commercial EDA tools. It derives role-compatible hybrid-bond (HB) sites from a 17-metal ASAP7-based technology model, complete HB footprints, and constructed PG geometry. To coordinate partitioning with placement flexibility, Scaled refines an inherited 2D placement, whereas Fresh places the receiving die first and uses its pin locations and clock loads to guide placement of the other die. Data and clock HB assignments are jointly optimized while retaining alternative data sites and reserving capacity for subsequent PG assignment. The selected HB sites and stacks are preserved during 3D clock-tree synthesis, supply-aware cell insertion, and routing. Across eleven designs, including a 133-macro processor, the flow achieves zero backend DRC violations and passes signal-connectivity checks. Nine paired designs admit lower-footprint, lower-power implementations; four improve setup WNS. On JPEG, early joint planning gains 87 ps and mobility-aware partitioning gains 346 ps. Path analysis explains why cell-delay savings can outweigh net-delay increases.

title: Practical Deep Learning-Based Block Demapping for mmWave MIMO Systems
comment: Submitted for publication to IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications
summary: Deep learning is expected to play a central role in 6G systems, by enabling data-driven physical layer designs that can adapt to practical wireless impairments. This is particularly important for millimetre-wave (mmWave) multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) systems, which are strongly affected by residual channel distortions, interference, and hardware non-idealities that are difficult to capture with analytical models. In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based soft demapper that performs block-wise processing of received symbols instead of conventional symbol-wise detection. The demapper employs a one-dimensional convolutional neural network to learn temporal structure induced by practical propagation and hardware effects, while producing soft bit outputs compatible with soft-decision decoding stages. The proposed approach is trained and evaluated for a 4$\times$4 wideband mmWave MIMO system at 60~GHz, using an over-the-air dataset collected across multiple days and settings. Experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements over a conventional soft-decision demapper, including up to a 2.6$\times$ reduction in bit error rate for 16QAM and up to a 17.6$\times$ reduction for 64QAM under real over-the-air mmWave MIMO conditions. The proposed demapper is further implemented on a Zynq RFSoC platform using a reconfigurable convolution engine and fixed-point arithmetic, achieving an approximately 34.3$\times$ speedup compared to a processor-based implementation, and demonstrating that learning-based demapping can be deployed efficiently on resource-constrained edge hardware.

title: AscSpMM: Efficient SpMM on Ascend NPUs via Pipelined Vector-Cube Collaboration
summary: Neural processing units (NPUs) provide high compute density and energy efficiency through specialized matrix engines and software-managed on-chip memory. However, their libraries primarily target dense computation. Sparse matrix-dense matrix multiplication (SpMM), a key kernel in graph analytics, sparse neural networks, and scientific computing, requires index-driven operand selection, indirect addressing, scattered memory accesses, and load balancing. These requirements conflict with the fixed shapes and contiguous layouts preferred by NPU matrix engines. GPU Tensor Core SpMM methods cannot be directly transferred to NPUs with decoupled vector and matrix engines. We present AscSpMM, which separates irregular operand preparation from regular matrix computation through a parameterized Vector-CSR representation. The vector engine decodes indices and gathers and reorganizes dense operands, while the Cube engine performs matrix multiply-accumulate operations. A double-slot ring buffer enables dependency-aware asynchronous pipelining, while operand reuse and runtime-adaptive tiling reduce cross-engine stalls. On an Ascend 910B3, AscSpMM achieves geometric-mean speedups of 2.36x over GEMM, 19.92x over an existing SpMM implementation, and 5.82x over cuSPARSE on an A100. It reduces matrix-input storage and peak HBM footprint by 48.24% and 22.98% on average, while remaining competitive with specialized GPU Tensor Core SpMM kernels. The code is available at https://github.com/LfLab-AI/Ascend-NPU-SpMM.

title: To SIMD or Not to SIMD: Comparing RVV vs. CGRA SoCs for Non-Linear Functions in AI
comment: Published in the H2RC workshop at the International Conference on High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis 2026
summary: Non-linear functions are an important class of operations in modern large language models. However, chip vendors building for AI have so far relied on traditional vector or scalar processing units for non-linear functions. The performance of these units has not kept pace with matrix multiplication units (MMUs), which can be found in both high-performance and edge-computing devices from almost every vendor. Reconfigurable units such as FPGAs and CGRAs have been proposed in the literature, but have not been systematically compared with traditional units backed by MMUs. In this paper, we build two SoCs: one using an RVV vector processor and the other using a latency-insensitive (\emph{elastic}) CGRA, both coupled with an MMU and driven by a single-core CPU. We then propose mappings for common feed-forward networks on our SoCs and find that the CGRA reaches a maximum speedup in clock cycles of 7.12x over RVV on the activation stage of simple point-wise non-linear functions like SiLU, whereas the RVV reaches a maximum speedup of \textbf{9.8x} over the CGRA on complex non-linear functions such as $\mathrm{softmax}$. Over the enclosing feed-forward block the corresponding maxima are 3.16x and 4.24x.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Privacy-Enhanced Computing Through Register Renaming
summary:
Privacy-Enhanced Computing (PEC) is a mechanism to hide program secrets from the outside world without paying the cost of fully-homomorphic encryption. Previous work has developed hardware mechanisms to achieve this goal but they require a dedicated processor enclave where all computations are done, requiring duplicate ALU resources and limiting the performance of PEC-utilizing applications due to not being able to access the full compute resources of the processor (e.g., multiple execution units and vector units), or not being able to execute PEC instructions in parallel and out-of-order.
  In this work, we introduce HPS-PEC (Hidden in Plain Sight PEC), a novel method of utilizing existing infrastructure in the CPU to achieve PEC with minor modifications to the architecture. We show that, across 25 VIP-Bench benchmarks and with a 7-cycle QARMA-64 cipher, HPS-PEC runs encrypted code at 3.41x the execution time of unprotected native code (geometric mean), of which 1.03x is the cost of data-oblivious code itself, and is 1.26x faster than a Sequestered Encryption (SE) unit while utilizing under a third of its dedicated area. Our method keeps plaintext out of reach of every instruction, as an enclave does given a correctly functioning renamer and register file, which every program already depends on.
